Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Ahmed is a 64-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been working as a politician for many years. He recently sought help due to increasing distress related to his experiences as a relief worker in a war zone. His traumatic experience left him with vivid and fragmented memories of the events, which continue to profoundly affect his daily life. During one particularly harrowing mission, Ahmed was caught in an explosion that killed several colleagues he had come to know well. The scent of burnt earth and smoke filled the air as the chaos unfolded around him. This moment remains seared into his memory; any olfactory trigger associated with a burnt smell instantly transports him back to those terrifying moments. The event has left Ahmed extremely sensitive to certain triggers that remind him of this traumatic experience. Talking to strangers, especially those who mention military topics, often provokes intense anxiety and discomfort. Whenever he encounters these situations, his emotional distress becomes overwhelming, prompting him to engage in maladaptive strategies such as trying hard to control his emotions or distracting himself with work. Ahmed’s attempts to manage his emotions through overworking have become a constant struggle. He throws himself into tasks and projects at work, keeping his mind occupied to avoid the intrusion of painful memories. However, this relentless focus on work has taken its toll, leading to significant strain in both his professional life and personal relationships. His colleagues notice that he is often distant and preoccupied, while friends and family feel increasingly shut out. The memories of the traumatic event continue to surface unexpectedly, bringing back the same terror Ahmed felt at the time. These intrusive recollections are fragmented, making it difficult for him to piece together a coherent narrative of what happened. When these memories return, they often overwhelm him with intense emotions that he finds impossible to process. This emotional turmoil reinforces his tendency to avoid anything that might trigger these memories further. The fear and anxiety associated with remembering the event have also led Ahmed to become hyper-vigilant about potential threats in his environment. Unusual silence makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen, leading him to repeatedly check doors and windows for security. This constant scanning for danger has become a pervasive part of his daily routine, creating a sense of unease that never fully dissipates. These feelings of threat are further exacerbated by his maladaptive strategies. As he tries to control his emotions or distract himself with work, the intensity of these intrusive memories increases, making it even more difficult to manage his anxiety. The cycle becomes self-reinforcing: Ahmed’s attempts to avoid triggers and control his emotional responses only serve to heighten his sense of threat. Recently, Ahmed realized that he could no longer maintain this constant state of hyper-vigilance without significant consequences. His work performance has suffered, as have his relationships with those around him. He is acutely aware that if he continues down this path, he will lose not only his job but also the support system he needs to cope. Ahmed’s most pressing concern now is finding a way to break free from this cycle of anxiety and avoidance. He hopes to regain control over his life and reconnect with those around him without feeling constantly on edge. Seeking therapy feels like a necessary step in addressing these issues, as he fears that the emotional burden will only become heavier if left unchecked. In summary, Ahmed’s traumatic experience has left him struggling with specific triggers, maladaptive coping mechanisms, heightened threat perceptions, and fragmented memories. The interplay between these components has created a self-reinforcing cycle of distress, ultimately driving him to seek help in hopes of regaining a sense of stability and control over his life.
